meta.description: No — van Gogh never wrote it. The line is painter Camille Corot's, documented in English by 1908; it was pinned on van Gogh only from the 1990s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I dream my painting, and then I paint my dream'?
meta.ogDescription: It's not van Gogh. The saying belongs to Camille Corot ('I dream my picture and afterwards I paint my dream'), in print by 1908 — reassigned to van Gogh in the 1990s.

answer.label: Not Vincent van Gogh — actually Camille Corot
answer.sourceLine: This line did not come from van Gogh at all. It is a lightly reworded English rendering of the painter Camille Corot’s remark — French: “Je rêve mon tableau, et plus tard je peindrai mon rêve” — documented in English print by 1908–1918. The Corot original reads “I dream my picture and afterwards I paint my dream.” The van Gogh version is unsourced and appears only from the 1990s onward; it is not found anywhere in van Gogh’s letters.

source.excerpt: Je rêve mon tableau, et plus tard je peindrai mon rêve. — “I dream my picture and afterwards I paint my dream.”
trail: Quote-database and gift-shop culture credits the line to Vincent van Gogh, but it is absent from his complete letters and from Wikiquote’s van Gogh entry.
The Wikiquote Corot entry documents the French original and English translations in sources from 1908 and 1918, and notes the van Gogh attribution is unsourced and dates only to the 1990s.
An early van Gogh misattribution appears in Jan Phillips, Marry Your Muse (1997), p. 176 — listed there as “undated.”
source.excerptNote: Corot’s remark, as translated in the Musical Courier (1908) and Thomas Troward’s Bible Mystery and Bible Meaning (1918). The popular “van Gogh” wording simply swaps picture→painting and afterwards→then.
source.rightsNote: The saying is Corot’s (d. 1875), and its documented English translations appeared in the Musical Courier (1908) and Thomas Troward’s Bible Mystery and Bible Meaning (1918) — all well before 1931 and firmly in the public domain. The popular “van Gogh” form is a trivial modern reword of that public-domain line, not a separately copyrightable work.

author.name: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot
author.heading: About Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot
author.metaLine: 1796–1875 · French landscape painter, leading figure of the Barbizon school
author.bio: Camille Corot was one of the most influential French landscape painters of the 19th century, a bridge between Neoclassical tradition and the Impressionism that followed. He was famous for his silvery, dreamlike woodland scenes and for the aphorisms about imagination and memory he shared with younger painters. The saying “I dream my picture and afterwards I paint my dream” captures his method of working from remembered impression rather than literal observation — and it is his line, not van Gogh’s.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: A clever aphorism about painting from imagination is exactly the kind of line that drifts toward the most famous name available. Van Gogh — endlessly quotable and endlessly quote-farmed — picked it up in the 1990s, and museums and merch have repeated it since.

items.why: Credited to van Gogh across quote sites, and even shared by the Van Gogh Museum — but with no letter, date, or source given, and it is absent from his writings. The earliest van Gogh attributions found date only to the 1990s.

misattribution.truthLine: The line belongs to Camille Corot — “Je rêve mon tableau, et plus tard je peindrai mon rêve” / “I dream my picture and afterwards I paint my dream” — documented in English by 1908, decades before it was ever pinned on van Gogh.

context.heading: Why the mix-up is easy
lead: Corot and van Gogh are cousins in spirit: both prized the remembered impression over slavish copying of nature, and both are quoted for it. Corot’s maxim about dreaming a picture and then painting the dream reads like something van Gogh could have written — which is precisely how misattributions stick.

But the paper trail is one-directional. Corot’s line is in English print by 1908; the van Gogh version surfaces only in the 1990s, always without a source. When a quote’s documented history predates its ‘famous author’ by nearly a century, the famous author is the borrower.
context.pull: Corot said it first — in print by 1908, eighty years before van Gogh got the credit.
